newsitem.title: CHINA: China banks see domestic competition growing.
newsitem.headline: China banks see domestic competition growing.

text.p: China's state banks are beginning to feel the cold wind of competition, both among themselves and from the handful of foreign banks newly given the right to do local currency business, bankers said on Friday.

The banks recognised a need to quickly improve their services and management, although the threat from foreign competitors was not immediate given the heavy restrictions they will initially be working under.
"Pressure is mounting now that the foreign banks have started doing renminbi (Chinese yuan) business," said one Beijing-based banker with a major state-run bank.
"Our management has lagged behind the foreign banks. We have so far been allowed to monopolise services to some extent, but we have to improve, and quickly," he added.
A senior official with a foreign bank in Shanghai said feedback from multi-national customers in particular indicated a change in attitude by many Chinese bank branches.
"The local banks are not very aggressive, but they are trying to be responsive, especially to the multi-nationals and other high-profile customers," the banker said.
"But it depends on the size of the bank and the quality of the human resources," he said. "Top of the list so far are joint-stock banks like Pudong Development bank and the Bank of Communications."

These two Shanghai-based banks are still state-owned but are smaller and more flexible than the major state banks, such as the Industrial and Commercial bank of China (ICBC), which have tens of thousands of branches nationwide, lack computerisation and whose transactions are bogged down by the red tape of central planning.

"ICBC is very large, so it's not able to move so quickly or in so concerted a way. But it varies from one branch to another. Some branch managers seem to be quite aggressive in this aspect," the foreign bank official said.

A total of eight foreign banks have so far won approval to handle yuan loans and deposits and several have already begun to do business, although on an experimental basis and with significant restrictions.

Bankers said competition among the domestic banks was becoming more noticeable, particularly with the expected dismantling over the next year or so of the current loan quota system for working capital up to one year.
"Many banks whose hands are tied by the current loan quota system will be free to lend to their best customers and will become much more competitive as a result," said the foreign banker.
Local bankers were keenly aware of the change.
"Competition is not only coming from foreign banks but is also intensifying among ourselves," the banker with a major Shanghai-based bank said.

"In Shanghai, for instance, we are seeing many banks from other regions registering, in particular those from southern China such as the Shenzhen Development Bank and Gudong Development Bank," she said.
Chinese bankers said they expected a large part of their business with foreign-funded firms in Shanghai eventually to be taken over by foreign banks.

"But we do not see an immediate threat," said one Shanghai-based banker with a major Chinese bank. "Business with foreign-funded firms is only a small part of our business and there are many restrictions (on the foreign banks)."
